head: 'Langley' means the long clearing.
text: It comes from Old English lang, long, and lēah, a clearing in a wood. The old village is sometimes called Langley Marish, after a family who held land here.

head: Named after Edward Latymer, a London merchant who died in 1627.
text: He left land here in his will to help poor people of Hammersmith, and his money also founded Latymer School. The road ran through his property. The station opened in 1868.

head: Named after the Earl of Leicester, who built Leicester House here.
text: The square was laid out in front of his house in the 1670s. The city of Leicester takes its name from a Celtic tribe and 'ceaster', a Roman town.

head: 'Lewisham' probably means the homestead of a man called Lēofsa.
text: The name ends in Old English hām, homestead. The River Ravensbourne and its tributary the Quaggy meet near the station.

head: 'Leyton' means the farm on the River Lea.
text: The Lea, or Lee, runs along the edge of the area. The station first opened in 1856 as Low Leyton and joined the Central line in 1947.

head: Named after Leyton, the farm on the River Lea, and the Midland Railway.
text: The railway company built the line through here in the 1890s, and the road beside the station took its name.

head: 'Leytonstone' means Leyton at the stone.
text: Leyton is the farm on the River Lea. The stone was probably an old Roman milestone or boundary stone near Hollybush Hill. Film director Alfred Hitchcock was born here in 1899.

head: 'Leytonstone' means Leyton at the stone.
text: Leyton is the farm on the River Lea; the stone was probably a Roman milestone or a boundary stone. The film director Alfred Hitchcock was born here in 1899.

head: 'Limehouse' means the lime kilns.
text: In the 14th century the name was 'lymhostes', the oasts or kilns where chalk was burnt to make lime for building. Later Limehouse was a busy port district.

head: Named after Lord Liverpool, Prime Minister from 1812 to 1827.
text: The street was named after him in the 1820s. His title comes from the city of Liverpool, first recorded in 1190 as Liuerpul, probably a pool or creek with muddy water. The station opened in 1875 as Bishopsgate.

head: Named after London Bridge, the oldest crossing of the Thames in the city.
text: There has been a bridge here since Roman times. The main line station opened in 1836 and is the oldest railway terminus in central London still in use.

head: Named after London City Airport, the airport nearest the City of London.
text: It opened in 1987 on the quay between two of the old Royal Docks. The DLR station followed in 2005.

head: Named after common fields where animals grazed on their way to London's markets.
text: Drovers rested their herds here before the last stretch into the City. The fields are now a park with an open-air pool.

head: 'Loughton' means the farm of a man called Luhha.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Lochintuna. Much older is Loughton Camp, an Iron Age earthwork in the forest nearby.

head: Named after a pub, the Hero of Maida, which recalled a battle in Italy.
text: In 1806 a British force under General Sir John Stuart beat the French at Maida, in Calabria. The pub opened beside the Edgware Road soon after, and the area took its name.

head: 'Maidenhead' means the landing place of the maidens.
text: It comes from Old English mægden, maiden, and hȳth, a landing place on the Thames. Brunel's railway bridge here, opened in 1838, has two of the widest and flattest brick arches ever built.

head: Named after the Manor House, a pub on Green Lanes.
text: The inn stood on the road to the north and gave its name to the crossroads. The station opened in 1932.

head: Named after the manor house of the manor of Little Ilford.
text: The area was farmland until houses were built in the late 19th century. The City of London Cemetery, one of the largest in Britain, is next door.

head: Named after Mansion House, the official home of the Lord Mayor of the City of London.
text: The grand house was built in the 18th century. Bank and Cannon Street stations are actually a little closer to it.

head: Named after the white marble arch designed by John Nash.
text: It was built in the 1820s as an entrance to Buckingham Palace and moved here in 1851. Nearby stood the Tyburn gallows, London's main place of execution for centuries.

head: Named after Maryland Point, said to recall the American colony of Maryland.
text: The name appears on a map of 1696. The story goes that a merchant who had made his fortune in Maryland built a house here, but this has not been proven. The colony itself was named after Queen Henrietta Maria.

head: 'Marylebone' means St Mary's church by the stream.
text: It was recorded in 1453 as Maryburne, after a church of St Mary by the Tyburn stream; the 'le' was added later. The station opened in 1907 as Great Central, after the railway company.

head: Named because it lies one mile from Aldgate, the old City gate.
text: The name has been used since the 13th century, for the place where the first mile of the road to Essex ended.

head: 'Mill Hill' probably means the hill with a windmill.
text: No trace of the mill remains, but a nearby field is still called Mill Field. The Northern line reached the station in 1941; it was meant to go further, but the extension was never built.

head: Named after the Monument to the Great Fire of London of 1666.
text: The column was designed by Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke. It is 61 metres tall, which is the distance from its base to the place in Pudding Lane where the fire began.

head: Named after Moor Park, a Palladian mansion nearby.
text: It stands on the site of an earlier house called The More, which belonged to Cardinal Wolsey. The station opened in 1910 as Sandy Lodge.

head: Named after the Moorgate, a small gate in the City wall.
text: It led out to Moorfields, marshy ground outside the wall. The gate was demolished in 1762.

head: 'Morden' probably means the hill in the marshland.
text: It comes from Old English mōr, marsh, and dūn, hill. Morden is the end of the Northern line and the southernmost station on the Underground.

head: Named after the Earl of Mornington, elder brother of the Duke of Wellington.
text: Richard Wellesley, 2nd Earl of Mornington, was Governor-General of India and Foreign Secretary. The station also gave its name to a famous nonsense game on the BBC radio comedy I'm Sorry I Haven't a Clue.

head: Named after a mud chute: mud dug out of Millwall Dock was pumped here.
text: The mud built up into a large mound. Today the land is Mudchute Park and Farm, one of the largest city farms in Europe.

head: 'Neasden' means the nose-shaped hill.
text: It comes from Old English næs, nose, and dūn, hill. The station opened in 1880 as Kingsbury & Neasden.

head: Probably named after a coaching inn, the New Cross, on the road to Kent and Dover.
text: The inn may have taken its name from an older wayside cross at the crossroads. Goldsmiths, part of the University of London, is next to the station.

head: Named after a toll gate on the road at New Cross.
text: Travellers on the turnpike road to Kent paid here. New Cross itself is probably named after a coaching inn.

head: 'Newbury' means the new manor.
text: The name is medieval. The station opened in 1947, when the Central line took over a branch railway.

head: Named after a row of nine elm trees.
text: The name was first recorded around 1645. Since 1974 the area has been home to New Covent Garden Market, and the station opened in 2021.

head: 'Acton' means the farm by the oak trees.
text: It comes from Old English āc, oak, and tūn, farm. The station opened in 1923, north of the old town centre.

head: 'Ealing' means the people of a Saxon called Gilla.
text: The name was first recorded around 700 as Gillingas. North Ealing station opened in 1903.

head: 'Greenwich' means the green harbour or trading place.
text: It was first recorded in the early 10th century. The station, opened in 1999, is about two miles north-east of Greenwich itself, next to what was built as the Millennium Dome.

head: 'Harrow' comes from Old English hearg, a heathen temple or shrine.
text: The shrine probably stood on Harrow Hill, where St Mary's Church stands today. North Harrow station opened in 1915.

head: 'Wembley' means the clearing of a Saxon called Wemba.
text: It ends in Old English leah, a clearing. Bakerloo trains have called here since 1917.

head: Named after the north fields of Ealing.
text: The fields were farmland until houses were built in the early 20th century. The station opened in 1908 as Northfield Halt.

head: 'Northolt' means the northern nook of land.
text: It comes from Old English north and healh, a corner or nook. Its partner to the south is Southall. The station opened on the Central line in 1948.

head: Named after Northwick Park, the open space beside the station.
text: The name is said to come from the Rushout family, who owned the farmland here and whose country seat was Northwick Park in the Cotswolds. The station opened in 1923 as Northwick Park & Kenton.

head: 'Northwood' means the wood to the north.
text: It was the wooded northern part of the old parish of Ruislip. The station opened in 1887.

head: Named after Northwood, the wood to the north of Ruislip, and its hills.
text: The station opened in 1933 for a new housing estate. Oddly, it stands a little lower than Northwood station.

head: 'Norwood' means the north wood, north of Croydon.
text: The Great North Wood once covered the hills here. Several railway lines meet at the junction.

head: 'Notting' probably means the people of a man called Cnotta.
text: The name was recorded from the 14th century in many spellings, such as Knottynghull. The 'gate' was a toll gate on the road to Uxbridge.

head: Named after Oakwood Park, which takes its name from the oaks of Enfield Chase.
text: Enfield Chase was a royal hunting ground. The station opened in 1933 as Enfield West and became Oakwood in 1946.

head: Named after the street, recorded as Ealdestrate around 1200.
text: The name simply means 'old street'; the road is probably Roman. Because of the many tech firms around it, the roundabout above the station is nicknamed Silicon Roundabout.

head: 'Osterley' probably means the clearing with a sheepfold.
text: It was first recorded in the 13th century. Osterley House was built for the merchant Sir Thomas Gresham in the 16th century and later remodelled by Robert Adam.

head: Named after the Oval cricket ground.
text: The name goes back to an oval-shaped street plan of the 1790s; the cricket ground was laid out inside it. Surrey County Cricket Club has played here since 1845.

head: A 'circus' is a round place where roads meet; there was never a circus.
text: It is the crossing of Oxford Street and Regent Street. Oxford Street was the main road west towards Oxford.

head: 'Paddington' means the farm of a man called Padda.
text: The name is Anglo-Saxon, with -ington meaning the settlement of someone's people. The station opened in 1863 on the first underground railway.
